title: Arjuna drops his bow
hook: a blank summer calendar, and a warrior who would rather do nothing
carry: karma yoga: do your work, let go of the fruits
tomorrow: who is a year of service really for? the circle is wider.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kundalini came home: up to a meeting at the crown, then back down the same road, because in tantra the everyday world is Shakti too. That closed the Tantras. Today a new stretch begins: karma, and a year of service.

A blank calendar for the summer, every square empty. It looks like freedom, and maybe a little like pressure: shouldn't some of those squares do some good? The Bhagavad Gita opens with a man who wants his squares empty. Arjuna, the great archer, stands in his chariot between two armies and sees his own teachers and cousins across the field. He drops his bow and sits down. Better to live by begging, he says, than to kill my teachers. I won't fight.
screen: `A BLANK SUMMER CALENDAR.` → `ARJUNA BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `HE DROPS HIS BOW: I WON'T FIGHT.`

segments.voice: His friend and charioteer is Krishna, and over the next chapters Krishna answers him. In chapter three Arjuna presses: if knowing is better than doing, why push me into this terrible action? Krishna's reply is blunt. No one can remain even a moment without acting; the strands of nature move everyone. Even keeping the body alive takes action. So stepping out isn't on offer. The only question is how to act. And his answer has a name, the teaching this week is built on: karma yoga, the path of action. Do the work that's yours, and do it without clinging to its fruits. This week makes it practical: a year of service, built this way, and the first step is surprising. It doesn't start with a grand new project. It starts with the work already on the calendar: the job, the meals, the care of a parent, the ride to school, done as karma yoga. Now a neighbor. In the Hebrew Bible, Ecclesiastes puts it this way in the King James Version: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." The same starting place: what's already in your hand. And an honest difference. Ecclesiastes gives its reason right after: in the grave there is no work, so act while you can. Krishna's reason is that no one can step out of acting at all, so let go of the fruits and act well. One urges because time runs out. The other, because action never stops.
screen: `NO ONE STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `KARMA YOGA: LET GO OF THE FRUITS.` · `START WITH THE WORK ALREADY YOURS.` · `ECCLESIASTES: WHAT THY HAND FINDETH.` · then, large: `TIME RUNS OUT, OR ACTION NEVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: Picture your week, square by square. Count on your fingers the things you already do that serve someone: a meal made, a ride given, a message answered, a shift worked. With each one, say inwardly, as many Hindus do after an act, Krishnarpanam astu, may this be an offering to Krishna. If you don't pray, say: this is for someone.
Karma: action, which no one can step out of. Karma yoga: doing the work that's yours, and letting go of the fruits.
Your line: karma yoga, do your work and let go of the fruits. A year of service starts with what's already on the calendar. See you in the morning.

howItsDone: Many Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's karma yoga as doing one's own daily work as an offering, without clinging to results, and some close an act with the words Krishnarpanam astu; service, seva, is woven into ordinary family and work life.
